No.47

I Keep Doing Good — Why Does Suffering Still Find Me?

When suffering comes, do not rush to doubt your good deeds or blame yourself; first tend to the suffering in front of you.

Author's record · translated; the Chinese original is authoritative

Open in reading mode →

🔶Inquiry to Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva

I asked Ksitigarbha Bodhisattva: Bodhisattva, I believe in cause and effect and do good to accumulate virtue, yet hardships keep coming one after another. At such times, should I doubt that I have not practiced enough, or doubt cause and effect itself?

🔶The Bodhisattva's Teaching

You do good and meet suffering; do not rush to doubt goodness, and do not rush to blame yourself. The principle of cause and effect is not that if you plant good today, there will be no suffering tomorrow.

The forming of a single result is the coming together of many conditions; the arrival of a single suffering is not born of one cause.

Past causes, present conditions, the actions of others and the changes of the world may all meet at this moment.

So doing good is not a bargain with heaven and earth.
Do not say: 'I have done good — why must I still suffer?'

If you trade goodness for smooth fortune, and smooth fortune does not come, the good heart retreats; such goodness still seeks something.

Yet neither should you, whenever suffering comes, blame yourself, saying: 'It must be that I have not practiced enough; my karmic obstacles must be deep.'

This too is attachment.
Some suffering is not because you are not good;
some hardship is not sent to punish you.

Birth, aging, sickness and death, meeting and parting, gain and loss — the world is impermanent, and all beings meet these things.

The benefit of practice is not a guarantee of a life without hardship, but that when suffering comes, you have a little less resentment than before and a little more clarity; you create a little less evil and give rise to a little more compassion. If you do good only to avoid suffering, when suffering comes your faith will waver.

If you know that good is simply what should be done, then even when adversity appears you still do not repay evil with evil;

only then do you know that your good roots are growing. As for cause and effect, do not understand it as an account book that rewards good and punishes evil. Good causes have good results, evil causes have evil results;

yet results ripen slowly or quickly, in plain sight or unseen, as conditions interweave — more than an ordinary person can see all at once.

If you are suffering, first deal with the suffering before you;

if it can be treated, treat it; if it can be changed, change it; if it can be avoided, avoid it; if you can seek help, seek help.

Do not, because you speak of cause and effect, leave suffering untreated; nor, because you meet suffering, conclude that doing good is useless. When suffering comes, there is no need to doubt cause and effect first, nor to doubt yourself first. First ask: 'In this situation, what can I do right now?' Where you can change, have the courage to change; where you cannot change, learn to bear it; where you should seek help, do not let practice take the place of seeking help. What you should truly observe is not: 'How much good have I done, and how much blessing has it bought?' but: 'After these hardships, is my heart clearer and more compassionate than before?' If so, though the suffering has not ended, you are already walking the Way.

🔶Plain Rendering

You do good yet meet hardship; do not rush to doubt your good deeds, and do not rush to blame yourself. The principle of cause and effect is not that if you plant a good cause today, there will be no pain tomorrow.

A single result takes many conditions coming together; a single hardship is not caused by one reason alone either.

Past causes, present conditions, other people's actions and changes in the world may all come together at the same moment.

So doing good is not making a deal with heaven and earth.
Do not say: "I have already done good — why am I still made to suffer?"

If you do good only to buy good fortune, then when good fortune does not come, your good heart fades; such goodness still wants something in return.

But neither should you blame yourself whenever hardship comes, saying: "It must be that I haven't practiced well enough; my karmic obstacles must be too heavy."

That too is a kind of attachment.
Some suffering is not because you are bad;
some difficulties are not there to punish you.

Birth, aging, sickness and death, meeting and parting, gaining and losing — the world is impermanent by nature, and every being meets these.

The benefit of practice is not a guarantee that your life will have no hardship; it is that when hardship comes, you have a little less resentment than before and a little more understanding; you create a little less harm and give rise to a little more compassion. If you do good only to avoid suffering, your faith will be shaken when suffering arrives.

If you know that doing good is simply right, and even when adversity appears you still do not repay harm with harm,

then you truly know that your good roots are growing. As for cause and effect, do not think of it as an account book of rewards and punishments. Good causes bring good results, and harmful causes bring harmful results;

but results ripen fast or slow, obviously or subtly, and conditions are so intertwined that ordinary people cannot see it all at once.

If you are facing hardship, deal with the problem in front of you first;

if you can see a doctor, see a doctor; if you can change something, change it; if you can avoid it, avoid it; if you can ask for help, ask for help.

Do not let the idea of cause and effect make you leave suffering untreated; and do not decide that doing good is useless just because you meet hardship. When hardship comes, there is no need to doubt cause and effect first, nor to doubt yourself first. First ask: "At this moment, what can I do now?" Where things can change, have the courage to change them; where they cannot, learn to accept them; where you need help, do not use "practice" as a substitute for asking for help. What you should truly look at is not: "How much good have I done, and how much blessing has it earned me?"

but: "After going through these hardships, is my heart clearer and more compassionate than before?" If so, then although the hardship is not over, you are already walking the path of practice.
